title: Motion lab — everything that moves, once each

slides.name: 1 · Statement · frame

params.text: Motion Lab / Movement with a purpose

slides.notes: Opening: one entrance, then rest. Motion should help the room locate, follow or connect information. Use the later looping example for waiting screens.

slides.name: 2 · Statement · frame

params.text: A gentle background supports the opening

slides.notes:
The same layout with more to say: the band steps the type down from 320 to 140px on its own. Backdrop: Drift — the blobs are this theme’s accent at low alpha, so the same slide in the paper theme is a pale wash rather than a glow.

Words: Rise, Medium, Wave. This is the default pairing.

slides.name: 3 · Statement · frame
slides.notes: Matched comparison: the wording, composition and effect stay the same. Only speed changes. Copy the slide and replace the phrase; keep the movement only if it helps your delivery.

slides.notes: Matched comparison: the wording, composition and effect stay the same. Only speed changes. Copy the slide and replace the phrase; keep the movement only if it helps your delivery.

slides.name: 5 · Statement · frame
slides.notes: Matched comparison: the wording, composition and effect stay the same. Only speed changes. Copy the slide and replace the phrase; keep the movement only if it helps your delivery.

slides.name: 6 · Statement · frame

params.text: Together / read the phrase as a whole

slides.notes: SPACING 1 of 2 — Together: every word carries the same delay of nothing, so the line arrives as a single movement. Effect here is Fade, so the only thing being demonstrated is the spacing.

slides.name: 7 · Statement · frame

params.text: One at a time / follow the sequence

slides.notes: SPACING 2 of 2 — One at a time: two and a half times the wave, which on six words is over a second and a half from first to last. Same Fade effect as the slide before; only the spacing changed.

slides.name: 8 · Statement · frame
slides.notes:
WAVE STARTS: the middle. Same spacing as the slide before — what changed is the order: the centre word leads and the wave opens to both ends at once (1625, 1271, 0, 1271, 1625 in milliseconds).

It reads as a phrase opening rather than a line being typed, which suits a statement that is one idea. First word and Last word are the other two.

slides.name: 9 · Statement · frame
slides.notes: The third effect: Reveal, a clip-path wipe rather than a move. Backdrop: Grid — a ruled plane travelling exactly one cell per loop, which is the same picture again, so it never cuts.

slides.name: 10 · Statement · frame
slides.notes: AND LEAVE AGAIN — the loop. Seven seconds: in for the first tenth, held for half, then nearly two seconds of the same eased wave taking them out, and a pause before it comes round. Stay here and watch it twice.

slides.name: 11 · Statement · frame
slides.notes:
ARC 1 of 3 — Bounce. Each word falls from above and goes PAST its resting place before coming back: out about 45px, back, out again smaller, then still. Measured, not approximated — the overshoot is a fraction of that word’s own drop, so the word that fell furthest bounces hardest.

Why it is not a preset: a start position eased to rest can only ever settle. The arc is a different keyframe set, chosen per word, which is why one word in a line can land like this while the rest do not.

slides.name: 12 · Statement · frame
slides.notes:
ARC 2 of 3 — Mist. The difference from a normal arrival is which property finishes last. These words are in position about half way through and still 50% out of focus; the rest of the time is spent condensing, which is what reads as coming out of fog rather than flying in slightly soft.

The arc supplies its own blur floor, so asking for mist without setting a blur still mists.

slides.name: 13 · Statement · frame
slides.notes:
ARC 3 of 3 — the unit itself. Nine steps for nine letters: the line is split by letter instead of by word, and each letter gets its own coordinates. The gap after "Charts" is the word break — 150ms rather than 90.

Each word is still one box, so the line can never break down the middle of a word. And the split is hidden from the accessibility tree with the sentence handed back whole underneath, because nineteen one-character elements are otherwise read out as "C h a r t s l i e". Thirty animated letters is the ceiling; past that it falls back to whole words.

slides.name: 14 · Full picture

params.text: Guide the eye through the image

slides.notes: Image motion: Travel. Pick a start point, an end point and a duration. This example uses a city photograph. Keep a chart still if the audience needs to compare values across it. Reduced-motion users receive a still image.

slides.name: 15 · A chart walked category by category

params.text: A chart walked category by category
Source: Every Santander Cycle hire, 2018–2023 · TfL, London Datastore

slides.notes:
CHART CALLOUTS. Press Next: the chart zooms to 2020 with its own axis label still in frame, then to 2023, then the whole chart comes back before the deck moves on.

Callouts name a CATEGORY from the table rather than a position, so inserting a row above 2020 does not move the callout. Add them in Design & content → Walk the chart.

slides.name: 16 · Reveal the reasoning.
slides.notes: Use Next to reveal each point. Earlier points remain in place so the audience can keep the argument in view. The printed version shows all points.

slides.name: 17 · Full picture
slides.notes:
Enhanced silk-light backdrop: twelve seconds, silent, with three independently blended light fields and two soft ribbons. Slow closed paths provide continuous movement; a vignette and quieter lower third leave room for the caption.

Loop, Start muted and Play when the slide appears are enabled. Choose caption style and position in Look. Regenerate using tools/video/backdrop-silk.py and the existing Swift encoder.

slides.name: 18 · Full picture
slides.notes:
Paste a watch link and the editor shows the video’s own thumbnail with a YOUTUBE pill on it, rather than the grey rectangle it used to draw — which was indistinguishable from a field that had ignored the link.

In the show this is the real player, framed from youtube-nocookie.com so nothing is set on a student’s machine until the clip is played.

slides.name: 19 · The same six years
slides.notes:
MORPH, 1 of 2. This slide and the next hold the same table and are set to Morph, so the chart itself travels across the cut rather than the slides dissolving.

Press Next slowly.

slides.name: 20 · The same six years

params.text: Source: Bars to a line, same numbers · TfL, London Datastore

slides.notes:
MORPH, 2 of 2 — and the argument for it: this is a claim about the material, not a decoration. The room is told “this is the same data, drawn the right way” by the fact that it moved rather than changed.

The browser does the animation; the app’s job is deciding what counts as the same thing — same picture, same chart table, or same heading text. With nothing shared it is a fade.

slides.name: 21 · Statement · frame

params.text: Morphed from the heading of the slide before

slides.notes:
The third pairing: the heading text is identical to the previous slide’s title, so the words themselves travel out of the chart slide and into the middle of this one.

Word effects are off here on purpose — a morph and an entrance both animating the same words fight each other.

slides.name: 22 · Statement · frame

params.text: Motion Lab / The data stays; the encoding moves

slides.notes:
A catalogue inside the catalogue. Everything after this slide is one slide type — Visual experiment — shown once per thing it can do.

The rule that separates it from the morph pair earlier: those two slides move a chart ACROSS a cut. An experiment moves it WITHIN one slide, under a prediction the room has already committed to. Add one with Add slide → Visual experiment.

slides.name: 23 · Pie slices become bars

params.text: Which candidate gains most across the polls?

params.data:
Candidate	Poll A	Poll B	Poll C
1	17	20	23
2	18	20	22
3	20	19	20
4	22	21	18
5	23	20	17
params.source: Illustrative teaching data — synthetic, not observed.
params.prompt: Which candidate gains most across the polls?

slides.notes:
PIE TO BAR — the headline. Press Next: the prediction prompt comes first, then one state at a time.

Watch a single slice. It does not fade out while a bar fades in; it is the same polygon re-cut, so a datum keeps its identity across the encoding. That is the whole argument for animating rather than cross-fading — the room can follow one candidate through the change.

The PDF fields on this slide are filled in as an example: Design & content → PDF: what changes / what stays fixed / key takeaway / limitations. A handout shows the final state, so those four lines are what carries the transformation onto paper.

slides.name: 24 · One dataset, five channels

params.text: Which encoding makes close quantities easiest to compare?

params.data:
Item	Value
A	20
B	24
C	38
D	42
params.source: Illustrative teaching data — synthetic, not observed.
params.prompt: Which encoding makes close quantities easiest to compare?

slides.notes:
MARKS AND CHANNELS. Four values pass through five encodings without being edited.

Area is the one to slow down for: radius follows the square root of the value, so the circle's AREA is the quantity. Hue and shape are identity channels — they say which, never how many, and the labels are doing the quantitative work on those two states.

Design & content → Visual, per state: bar, pie, line, dot, bubbles, hue, shape, tiles, table, network, field, geometry, classification.

slides.name: 25 · Hide the values, then reveal them

params.text: Hide the values, then reveal them
Estimate B as a percentage of A. Say a number before you see the next state.

params.states: [{"label":"Judge area","kind":"bubbles","hideValues":true,"explanation":"Circle area — not radius — carries the value. Commit to a number and keep it."},{"label":"Aligned lengths","kind":"bar","categorical":true,"hideValues":true,"explanation":"The same two values against a shared zero. Revise your estimate only if this encoding gives you better evidence."},{"label":"Reveal the values","kind":"bar","categorical":true,"explanation":"A = 40 and B = 30, so B is 75% of A. Which encoding got you closer?"}]
params.source: Two synthetic values chosen for the estimate.
params.prompt: Estimate B as a percentage of A. Say a number before you see the next state.

slides.notes:
HIDE VALUES. Each state has its own checkbox — Design & content → Hide values for an estimation challenge — so you can strip the labels for two states and hand them back on the third.

This is what makes the prediction prompt worth having. Without it the room reads the answer off the chart and predicts nothing.

Say the caveat out loud: this is a classroom experience, not a controlled perception study, and it does not rank chart types universally.

slides.name: 26 · The baseline moves under fixed values

params.text: The baseline moves under fixed values
The values stay at 100 and 110. How much bigger does the second bar look?

params.source: Illustrative teaching data — synthetic, not observed.
params.prompt: The values stay at 100 and 110. How much bigger does the second bar look?

slides.notes:
AXIS MINIMUM. The bars grow and shrink while the data sits still — the number moving is the axis minimum, and the axis labels travel with it.

Design & content → Axis minimum, per state, for bar, line and dot. The distortion here is deliberate and labelled as such in the explanations; keep it that way. Lie factor 10, then 20, then zero restored.

A bar encodes length. Cutting the baseline breaks the relationship between length and quantity, which is why this one is a bar rather than a line.

slides.name: 27 · Narrower plot, chosen ending

params.text: Can the same observations appear to tell different stories?

params.source: Illustrative teaching data — synthetic, not observed.
params.prompt: Can the same observations appear to tell different stories?

slides.notes:
ASPECT RATIO AND SELECTED RANGE. Neither state edits a value. The second squeezes the plot so the slopes steepen; the third starts at period 4 so the series appears to decline.

This is the companion to the baseline slide: that one distorts the scale, this one distorts the shape and the window. Both are labelled distortions, shown to be recognised rather than copied.

slides.name: 28 · Decoration leaves before the data does

params.text: Decoration leaves before the data does
What gets your attention before you can compare the values?

params.data:
Day	Hires
Mon	42
Tue	58
Wed	47
Thu	70
Fri	64
params.source: Illustrative teaching data — synthetic, not observed.
params.prompt: What gets your attention before you can compare the values?

slides.notes:
PROGRESSIVE DECLUTTER. Decoration fades on its own track, separately from the data, so the room sees removal as an action rather than as a redraw.

Watch what stays: direct labels and a quiet baseline survive all three states, because they support the comparison. The lesson is not "less ink" — it is that the ink has to earn the attention it takes.

Design & content → Show deliberate clutter, per bar state.

slides.name: 29 · Fixed tiles, changing ramp

params.text: Which palette expresses the structure of each attribute?

params.data:
Region	Count	Change
North	20	-12
East	45	-4
South	70	5
West	95	16
params.source: Illustrative teaching data — synthetic, not observed.
params.prompt: Which palette expresses the structure of each attribute?

slides.notes:
PALETTE INTERPOLATION. The tiles do not move. Only their fill travels, so the change is unmistakably about colour and not about layout or order.

Design & content → Palette, on any tiles state: categorical, sequential, diverging. The third and fourth states also switch which attribute is shown — counts to signed change — which is the case for a diverging ramp: it needs a meaningful zero to depart from.

Ordinal levels are ranks. A sequential ramp orders them; it does not claim the gaps are equal.

slides.name: 30 · Take the colour away

params.text: Can you still identify each group when the colour disappears?

params.data:
Group	Value
North	20
East	24
South	38
West	42
params.source: Illustrative teaching data — synthetic, not observed.
params.prompt: Can you still identify each group when the colour disappears?

slides.notes:
GREYSCALE. Two states, and the second removes the colour entirely.

Position and direct labels carry the meaning through. That is the point: colour should be a redundant cue, not the only one.

Design & content → Greyscale, per bar state. Say the limit plainly — this is a demonstration of redundant encoding, not a colour-vision-deficiency simulator.

slides.name: 31 · Table, network, field, geometry

params.text: What is an item, a link, a field or a spatial boundary?

params.data:
Station	Hires
A	20
B	35
C	60
D	80
params.source: Illustrative teaching data — synthetic, not observed.
params.prompt: What is an item, a link, a field or a spatial boundary?

slides.notes:
DATASET STRUCTURES. The four shapes data arrives in, stepped through in one slide so the room can compare them rather than meet them ten minutes apart.

Each one answers a different question about what an item is: a row, a node, a sampled location, a boundary. Links need their own data — the network state says so in its explanation.

Field and geometry are illustrative presets. They are not GIS, not measured, and not real boundaries.

slides.name: 32 · Nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio

params.text: Do the values have order, meaningful differences, or meaningful ratios?

params.source: Illustrative teaching data — synthetic, not observed.
params.prompt: Do the values have order, meaningful differences, or meaningful ratios?

slides.notes:
ATTRIBUTE CLASSIFICATION. A text state rather than a chart state — kind: classification, with an example string per state.

It earns its place in a motion catalogue by being the same slide four times: the frame holds and only the example and its explanation change, so the four levels read as one scale instead of four bullets.

Station 12 is not four times Station 3; 20°C is not twice 10°C; twenty hires is twice ten.

slides.name: 33 · Overview, detail, overview

params.text: What changes when we focus on part of the series?

params.data:
Day	Hires
Mon	20
Tue	38
Wed	32
Thu	70
Fri	64
Sat	90
params.source: Illustrative teaching data — synthetic, not observed.
params.prompt: What changes when we focus on part of the series?

slides.notes:
OVERVIEW AND DETAIL. Three states: the whole series, a labelled detail, then the whole series again.

This is not free chart zoom — it filters to a labelled range, holds the vertical scale fixed, and returns. The return matters: a detail shown without its context is the selected-range distortion from earlier in this section.

Design & content → the detail state carries the starting point.

slides.name: 34 · The same change, slowed down

params.text: Which candidate gains most across the polls?

params.data:
Candidate	Poll A	Poll B	Poll C
1	17	20	23
2	18	20	22
3	20	19	20
4	22	21	18
5	23	20	17
params.source: Illustrative teaching data — synthetic, not observed.
params.prompt: Which candidate gains most across the polls?

slides.notes:
PACE AND REPLAY — the second half of the pie-to-bar pair. This is the same preset as the slide that opened this section, set to the slow pace.

Design & content → Transformation pace: Quick 0.8s, Teaching 1.6s, Slow observation 3s. Quick for a change the room already expects; slow for the one you want them to narrate while it happens.

Replay change retraces the last transition without stepping back a state, so you can answer "can we see that again" without losing your place. The state buttons jump straight to any state, or back to the prediction.

Reduced-motion settings are respected: those users get the settled states with no travel between them, which is why every explanation has to make sense standing still.
